The history of '''agriculture in India''' dates back to the [[South Asian Stone Age|Neolithic period]]. India [[List of countries by GDP sector composition|ranks]] second worldwide in farm outputs. As per the Indian economic survey 2020–21, agriculture employed more than 50% of the Indian workforce and contributed 20.2% to the country's GDP.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.financialexpress.com/budget/india-economic-survey-2018-for-farmers-agriculture-gdp-msp/1034266/|title=India economic survey 2018: Farmers gain as agriculture mechanisation speeds up, but more R&D needed|date=29 January 2018|website=The Financial Express|access-date=8 January 2019|archive-date=8 January 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190108200706/https://www.financialexpress.com/budget/india-economic-survey-2018-for-farmers-agriculture-gdp-msp/1034266/|url-status=live}}</ref>

== Definition of farmer ==
Indian farmers are people who grow crops as a profession.<ref name=":0"/> Various government estimates ([[Census of India|Census]], [[Census of agriculture|Agricultural Census]], [[National Sample Survey Office (India)|National Sample Survey]] assessments, and Periodic Labour Force Surveys) give a different number of farmers in the country ranging from 37 million to 118 million as per the different definitions.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|last=Agarwal|first=Kabir|date=9 March 2021|title=Indian Agriculture's Enduring Question: Just How Many Farmers Does the Country Have?|url=https://thewire.in/agriculture/indian-agricultures-enduring-question-just-how-many-farmers-does-the-country-have|access-date=22 March 2021|website=The Wire|archive-date=10 March 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210310073147/https://thewire.in/agriculture/indian-agricultures-enduring-question-just-how-many-farmers-does-the-country-have|url-status=live}}</ref> Some definitions take into account the number of holdings as compared to the number of farmers.<ref name=":1" /> Other definitions take into account possession of land, while others try to delink land ownership from the definition of a farmer.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|last=Choudhary|first=Nitu|date=9 December 2020|title=Who is a farmer? What is The Government's Definition Of A Farmer?|url=https://smarteklavya.com/governments-definition-of-a-farmer-in-india/|access-date=22 March 2021|website=Smart Eklavya|language=en-GB|archive-date=11 April 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210411222000/https://smarteklavya.com/governments-definition-of-a-farmer-in-india/}}</ref> Other terms also used include 'cultivator'.<ref name=":2" />

India's National Policy for Farmers 2007 defines farmer as:<ref name=":0">[https://agricoop.nic.in/sites/default/files/npff2007%20%281%29.pdf National Policy for Farmers] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200724161352/http://agricoop.nic.in/sites/default/files/npff2007%20%281%29.pdf |date=24 July 2020 }}. ''Department of Agriculture & Cooperation, Ministry of Agriculture, Government of India''. pp 4. Accessed on 22 March 2021.</ref>
{{Blockquote|text=For the purpose of this Policy, the term "FARMER" will refer to a person actively engaged in the economic and/or livelihood activity of growing crops and producing other primary agricultural commodities and will include all agricultural operational holders, cultivators, agricultural labourers, sharecroppers, tenants, poultry and livestock rearers, fishers, beekeepers, gardeners, pastoralists, non-corporate planters and planting labourers, as well as persons engaged in various farmingrelated occupations such as sericulture, vermiculture, and agro-forestry. The term will also include tribal families / persons engaged in shifting cultivation and in the collection, use and sale of timber and non-timber forest produce.}}
However this definition has not been adopted.<ref name=":0" />

As per the 2014 [[Food and Agriculture Organization|FAO]] world agriculture statistics India is the world's largest producer of many fresh [[fruit]]s like banana, mango, guava, papaya, [[lemon]] and vegetables like chickpea, okra and [[milk]], major [[spice]]s like chili pepper, ginger, fibrous crops such as [[jute]], staples such as [[millet]]s and [[castor oil]] seed. India is the second largest producer of [[wheat]] and [[rice]], the world's major [[staple food|food staples]].<ref name="faostat.fao.org">{{cite web|url=http://faostat.fao.org/site/567/default.aspx#ancor|title=FAOSTAT, 2014 data|publisher=Faostat.fao.org|access-date=17 September 2011|archive-date=7 April 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120407180211/http://faostat.fao.org/site/567/default.aspx#ancor}}</ref>

India is currently the world's second largest producer of several [[dried fruit|dry fruits]], agriculture-based [[textile]] raw materials, [[List of root vegetables|roots]] and [[tuber]] crops, [[Pulse (legume)|pulses]], farmed [[Fish (food)|fish]], [[Egg (food)|eggs]], [[coconut]], [[sugarcane]] and numerous [[vegetable]]s. India is ranked under the world's five largest producers of over 80% of agricultural produce items, including many [[cash crop]]s such as [[coffee]] and [[cotton]], in 2010.<ref name="faostat.fao.org"/> India is one of the world's five largest producers of [[livestock]] and [[poultry meat]], with one of the fastest growth rates, {{as of|2011|lc=y}}.<ref>{{cite web|title=Livestock and Poultry: World Markets & Trade|publisher=United States Department of Agriculture|date=October 2011|url=https://apps.fas.usda.gov/psdonline/circulars/livestock_poultry.pdf|access-date=28 December 2011|archive-date=11 October 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121011213233/http://www.fas.usda.gov/psdonline/circulars/livestock_poultry.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref>

One report from 2008 claimed that India's population is growing faster than its ability to produce rice and wheat.<ref name="nytagriculture">{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2008/06/22/business/22indiafood.html?_r=1|title=The Food Chain in Fertile India, Growth Outstrips Agriculture|work=The New York Times|date=22 June 2008|first=Somini|last=Sengupta|access-date=23 April 2010|archive-date=23 July 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140723172723/http://www.nytimes.com/2008/06/22/business/22indiafood.html?_r=1|url-status=live}}</ref> While other recent studies claim that India can easily feed its growing population, plus produce wheat and rice for global exports, if it can reduce food staple spoilage/wastage, improve its infrastructure and raise its farm productivity like those achieved by other developing countries such as [[Brazil]] and [[China]].<ref name=fao1a/><ref name=wboverview2/>

In fiscal year ending June 2011, with a normal monsoon season, Indian agriculture accomplished an all-time record production of 85.9 million tonnes of wheat, a 6.4% increase from a year earlier. Rice output in India hit a new record at 95.3 million tonnes, a 7% increase from the year earlier.<ref name=bloomberg1>{{cite web|title=India Allows Wheat Exports for the First Time in Four Years|date=8 September 2011|publisher=Bloomberg L.P.|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/2011-09-08/india-allows-wheat-exports-for-the-first-time-in-four-years-1-.html}}</ref> Lentils and many other food staples production also increased year over year. Indian farmers, thus produced about 71 kilograms of wheat and 80 kilograms of rice for every member of Indian population in 2011. The per capita supply of rice every year in India is now higher than the per capita consumption of rice every year in Japan.<ref>{{cite web|title=Fish and Rice in the Japanese Diet|year=2006|publisher=Japan Review|url=http://www.japanreview.net/essays_fish_and_rice.htm|access-date=21 December 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120406190801/http://www.japanreview.net/essays_fish_and_rice.htm|archive-date=6 April 2012}}</ref>

India exported $39 billion worth of agricultural products in 2013, making it the seventh largest agricultural exporter worldwide, and the sixth largest net exporter.<ref name=usda2014/> This represents explosive growth, as in 2004 net exports were about $5 billion.<ref name=usda2014/> India is the fastest growing exporter of agricultural products over a 10-year period, its $39 billion of net export is more than double the combined exports of the European Union (EU-28).<ref name="usda2014" /> It has become one of the world's largest supplier of rice, cotton, sugar and wheat. India exported around 2 million metric tonnes of wheat and 2.1 million metric tonnes of rice in 2011 to [[Africa]], [[Nepal]], [[Bangladesh]] and other regions around the world.<ref name=bloomberg1/>

[[Fishing in India|Aquaculture and catch fishery]] is among the fastest growing industries in India. Between 1990 and 2010, the Indian fish capture harvest doubled, while aquaculture harvest tripled. In 2008, India was the world's sixth largest producer of marine and freshwater capture fisheries and the second largest aquaculture farmed fish producer. India exported 600,000 metric tonnes of fish products to nearly half of the world's countries.<ref>{{cite web|title=The state of world fisheries and aquaculture, 2010|year=2010|publisher=FAO of the United Nations|url=http://www.fao.org/docrep/013/i1820e/i1820e.pdf|access-date=22 December 2011|archive-date=15 September 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110915222055/http://www.fao.org/docrep/013/i1820e/i1820e.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Export of marine products from India (see statistics section) |publisher=Central Institute of Fisheries Technology, India |year=2008 |url=http://www.cift.res.in/innercontent.php?contentid=MTgw |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130701054320/http://www.cift.res.in/innercontent.php?contentid=MTgw |archive-date=1 July 2013 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Fishery and Aquaculture Country Profiles: India|year=2011|publisher=Food and Africulture Organisation of the United Nations|url=http://www.fao.org/fishery/countrysector/FI-CP_IN/3/en|access-date=22 December 2011|archive-date=13 June 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120613175755/http://www.fao.org/fishery/countrysector/FI-CP_IN/3/en|url-status=live}}</ref> Though the available nutritional standard is 100% of the requirement, India lags far behind in terms of [[Essential amino acid|quality protein]] intake at 20% which is to be tackled by making available protein rich food products such as eggs, meat, fish, chicken etc. at affordable prices<ref name="India: Global Food Security Index">{{Cite web|url=http://foodsecurityindex.eiu.com/Country/Details#India|title=India: Global Food Security Index|access-date=17 January 2018|archive-date=12 July 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120712235613/http://foodsecurityindex.eiu.com/Country/Details#India}}</ref>

India has shown a steady average nationwide annual increase in the mass-produced per hectare for some agricultural items, over the last 60 years. These gains have come mainly from India's [[Green Revolution|green revolution]], improving road and power generation infrastructure, knowledge of gains and reforms.<ref name=rbi1/> Despite these recent accomplishments, agriculture has the potential for major productivity and total output gains, because crop yields in India are still just 30% to 60% of the best sustainable crop yields achievable in the farms of developed and other developing countries.<ref name=OSU2009>{{cite web|title=World Wheat, Corn and Rice |publisher=Oklahoma State University, FAOSTAT |url=http://nue.okstate.edu/crop_information/world_wheat_production.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150610121002/http://www.nue.okstate.edu/Crop_Information/World_Wheat_Production.htm |archive-date=10 June 2015 }}</ref> Additionally, post harvest losses due to poor infrastructure and unorganised retail, caused India to experience some of the highest food losses in the world.<ref name=Econ312>{{cite news|title=Indian retail: The supermarket's last frontier|newspaper=The Economist|date=3 December 2011|url=https://www.economist.com/business/2011/12/03/the-supermarkets-last-frontier|access-date=28 December 2011|archive-date=31 March 2024|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240331170933/https://www.economist.com/business/2011/12/03/the-supermarkets-last-frontier|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Emerging Trends, Challenges and Opportunities presentation, on publications page, see slides 7 through 21|author=Sinha, R.K.|publisher=National Seed Association of India|year=2010|url=http://www.nsai.co.in/Publication/exec/frmAllPublication.aspx?cID=Presentations|access-date=28 December 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111115152923/http://nsai.co.in/Publication/exec/frmAllPublication.aspx?cID=Presentations|archive-date=15 November 2011}}</ref>

[[File:Kurmi zamindars.png|thumb|Kurmi farmers of rural [[Bihar]] have started using modern agriculture technology]]
One of India's major agricultural products, rice, is suffering as a result of shifting monsoon patterns. States in the East of the country ([[Uttar Pradesh]], [[Bihar]], and [[Odisha]]), have experienced high temperatures and insufficient rainfall in 2022, in contrast to [[Central India|Central]] and [[South India|Southern India]], which has experienced excessive rain in recent months, resulting in flooding in the Southern states of [[Kerala]], [[Karnataka]], and [[Madhya Pradesh]].<ref name=":02">{{Cite web |title=India sustainable rice cuts water use and emissions |url=https://www.eib.org/en/stories/sustainable-rice-india |access-date=23 December 2022 |website=European Investment Bank |language=en |archive-date=23 December 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221223135242/https://www.eib.org/en/stories/sustainable-rice-india |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Deshpande |first=Tanvi |date=11 October 2021 |title=Climate Change Is Making India's Monsoon More Erratic |url=https://www.indiaspend.com/earthcheck/climate-change-is-making-indias-monsoon-more-erratic-780356 |access-date=23 December 2022 |website=www.indiaspend.com |language=en |archive-date=23 December 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221223135242/https://www.indiaspend.com/earthcheck/climate-change-is-making-indias-monsoon-more-erratic-780356 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name=":12">{{Cite news |last=Koshy |first=Jacob |date=25 September 2022 |title=Explained {{!}} Shifting monsoon patterns |language=en-IN |work=The Hindu |url=https://www.thehindu.com/sci-tech/energy-and-environment/shifting-monsoon-patterns/article65935590.ece |access-date=23 December 2022 |issn=0971-751X |archive-date=23 December 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221223135242/https://www.thehindu.com/sci-tech/energy-and-environment/shifting-monsoon-patterns/article65935590.ece |url-status=live }}</ref>

The rice crop this season is therefore anticipated to decrease by roughly 6.77 million tonnes to 104.99 million, according to India's ministry of agriculture.<ref name=":02" /><ref name=":12" />

A study on India's food and land-use systems highlights the need for improved skills, stronger institutional linkages, and increased research investment to enhance sustainability and resilience in agriculture.<ref>{{cite web |title=Food and Land Use Coalition Engagement in India - Phase II |url=https://www.teriin.org/project/food-and-land-use-coalition-engagement-india-phase-ii |website=TERI |access-date=31 March 2021}}</ref>

==History==
{{More citations needed|date=April 2016}}
{{main|History of agriculture in India}}
[[File:Farmers and Water Buffalo Plowing a Rice Field by Frank Bond.jpg|thumb|Farmers and [[Water buffalo|Water Buffalo]] Plowing a Rice Field, West Bengal, 1944]]
[[Vedic literature]] provides some of the earliest written record of agriculture in India. [[Rigveda]] hymns, for example, describes ploughing, fallowing, irrigation, fruit and vegetable cultivation. Other historical evidence suggests rice and cotton were cultivated in the [[Indus Valley]], and ploughing patterns from the [[Bronze Age]] have been excavated at [[Kalibangan]] in [[Rajasthan]].<ref name=pbs7>{{cite web|title=The Story of India: a PBS documentary|publisher=Public Broadcasting Service, United States|url=https://www.pbs.org/thestoryofindia/gallery/photos/7.html|access-date=23 August 2017|archive-date=25 August 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170825190252/http://www.pbs.org/thestoryofindia/gallery/photos/7.html|url-status=live}}</ref> Bhumivargaha, an Indian [[Sanskrit]] text, suggested to be 2500 years old, classifies agricultural land into 12 categories: urvara (fertile), ushara (barren), maru (desert), aprahata (fallow), shadvala (grassy), pankikala (muddy), jalaprayah (watery), kachchaha (contiguous to water), sharkara (full of pebbles and pieces of limestone), sharkaravati (sandy), nadimatruka (watered from a river), and devamatruka (rainfed). Some archaeologists believe that rice was a domesticated crop along the banks of the river Ganges in the sixth millennium BC.<ref>{{Cite journal |title=Agriculture in the Vedic Period |first=Mira |last=Roy |url=https://insa.nic.in/writereaddata/UpLoadedFiles/IJHS/Vol44_4_2_MRoy.pdf |journal=Indian Journal of History of Science |volume=44 |issue=4 |date=2009 |pages=497–520 |access-date=14 January 2019 |archive-date=25 August 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200825161613/https://insa.nic.in/writereaddata/UpLoadedFiles/IJHS/Vol44_4_2_MRoy.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref> So were species of winter cereals (barley, oats, and wheat) and legumes (lentil and chickpea) grown in northwest India before the sixth millennium BC.{{citation needed|date=April 2016}} Other crops cultivated in India 3000 to 6000 years ago, include sesame, linseed, safflower, mustard, castor, mung bean, black gram, horse gram, pigeon pea, field pea, grass pea (khesari), fenugreek, cotton, jujube, grapes, dates, jack fruit, mango, mulberry, and black plum{{citation needed|date=April 2016}}. Indians may have domesticated river buffalo 5000 years ago.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Indian Agriculture and IFFCO |url=https://www.craaq.qc.ca/documents/files/Evenements/EPER1401/08_Gupta_Manish_ang.pdf |website=Quebec Reference Center for Agriculture and Agri-food |access-date=14 January 2019 |archive-date=14 January 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190114153418/https://www.craaq.qc.ca/documents/files/Evenements/EPER1401/08_Gupta_Manish_ang.pdf |url-status=live }}</ref>

According to some scientists agriculture was widespread in the Indian peninsula, 10000–3000 years ago, well beyond the fertile plains of the north. ===Indian agriculture after independence===
Despite some stagnation during the later modern era the independent [[Republic of India]] was able to develop a comprehensive agricultural programme.<ref name="roy2006">Roy 2006</ref><ref name="kumar2006">Kumar 2006</ref>[[File:Tractor at Cotton Harvest.jpg|alt=|thumb|blueberry flower harvesting in India. This is a cash crop in [[Gujarat|Central Gujarat, India]].]]
In the years since its independence, India has made immense progress towards food security. Indian population has tripled, and food-grain production more than quadrupled. There has been a substantial increase in available food-grain per capita.
[[File:Rice fields water tank in punjab.jpg|alt=|left|thumb|250x250px|The state of [[Punjab (India)|Punjab]] led India's [[Green Revolution]] and earned the distinction of being the country's bread basket.<ref name=":3">{{cite report |url=http://planningcommission.nic.in/plans/stateplan/sdr_pdf/shdr_pun04.pdf |title=Human Development Report 2004, Punjab |date=2004 |author=[[Government of Punjab, India|The Government of Punjab]] |access-date=9 August 2011| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20110708073911/http://planningcommission.nic.in/plans/stateplan/sdr_pdf/shdr_pun04.pdf| archive-date= 8 July 2011 | url-status= live}} Section: "The Green Revolution", pp. 17–20.</ref>]]
Before the mid-1960s, India relied on imports and food aid to meet domestic requirements. However, two years of severe drought in 1965 and 1966 convinced India to reform its agricultural policy and that it could not rely on foreign aid and imports for food security. India adopted significant policy reforms focused on the goal of food grain self-sufficiency. This ushered in India's [[Green Revolution]]. It began with the decision to adopt superior yielding, disease resistant wheat varieties in combination with better farming knowledge to improve productivity. The state of [[Punjab (India)|Punjab]] led India's [[Green Revolution|green revolution]] and earned the distinction of being the country's breadbasket.<ref name=":3" />

The initial increase in production was centred on the irrigated areas of the states of [[Punjab, India|Punjab]], [[Haryana]] and western [[Uttar Pradesh]]. With the farmers and the government officials focusing on farm productivity and knowledge transfer, India's total food grain production soared. A hectare of Indian wheat farm that produced an average of 0.8 tonnes in 1948, produced 4.7 tonnes of wheat in 1975 from the same land. Such rapid growth in farm productivity enabled India to become self-sufficient by the 1970s. It also empowered the smallholder farmers to seek further means to increase food staples produced per hectare. By 2000, Indian farms were adopting wheat varieties capable of yielding 6 tonnes of wheat per hectare.<ref name=fao1a>{{cite web|title=Rapid growth of select Asian economies|year=2009|publisher=Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations|url=http://www.fao.org/docrep/009/ag087e/AG087E05.htm|access-date=19 December 2011|archive-date=13 September 2024|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240913065205/https://www.fao.org/4/ag087e/AG087E05.htm|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Brief history of wheat improvement in India|year=2011|publisher=Directorate of Wheat Research, ICAR India|url=http://www.dwr.in/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=1&Itemid=116|access-date=20 December 2011|archive-date=17 November 2011|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111117053227/http://www.dwr.in/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=1&Itemid=116|url-status=live}}</ref>

[[File:Sunflower farm, Agriculture in India, January 2013.jpg|alt=|thumb|Sunflower farm in Lepakshi, Andhra Pradesh]]

With agricultural policy success in wheat, India's Green Revolution technology spread to rice. However, since irrigation infrastructure was very poor, Indian farmers innovated with tube-wells, to harvest [[ground water]]. When gains from the new technology reached their limits in the states of initial adoption, the technology spread in the 1970s and 1980s to the states of eastern India — [[Bihar]], [[Odisha]] and [[West Bengal]]. The lasting benefits of the improved seeds and new technology extended principally to the irrigated areas which account for about one-third of the harvested crop area. In the 1980s, Indian agriculture policy shifted to "evolution of a production pattern in line with the demand pattern" leading to a shift in emphasis to other agricultural commodities like oilseed, fruit and vegetables. Farmers began adopting improved methods and technologies in dairying, fisheries and livestock, and meeting the diversified food needs of a growing population.

As with rice, the lasting benefits of improved seeds and improved farming technologies now largely depends on whether India develops infrastructure such as irrigation network, flood control systems, reliable electricity production capacity, all-season rural and urban highways, cold storage to prevent spoilage, modern retail, and competitive buyers of produce from Indian farmers. This is increasingly the focus of Indian agriculture policy.

India ranks 74 out of 113 major countries in terms of [[Global food security index|food security index]].<ref name="India: Global Food Security Index"/> India's agricultural economy is undergoing structural changes. Between 1970 and 2011, the GDP share of agriculture has fallen from 43% to 16%. This isn't because of reduced importance of agriculture or a consequence of agricultural policy; rather, it is largely due to the rapid economic growth in services, industrial output, and non-agricultural sectors in India between 2000 and 2010.

Agricultural scientist [[MS Swaminathan]] has played a vital role in the green revolution. In 2013, NDTV named him one of 25 living legends of India for outstanding contributions to agriculture and making India a food-sovereign country.{{Citation needed|date=July 2024}}

{{as of|2011}}, India had a large and diverse agricultural sector, accounting, on average, for about 16% of GDP and 10% of export earnings. India's arable land area of {{convert|159.7|e6ha|e6acre|abbr=off}} is the second largest in the world, after the United States. India is among the top three global producers of many crops, including wheat, rice, pulses, cotton, peanuts, fruits and vegetables. ===Organic agriculture===
====History====
[[Organic farming|Organic agriculture]] is the practice of using ecologically based [[Manure|manures]] and [[compost]] to cultivate [[Organic food|food]]. It prohibits the use of any synthetic [[Fertilizer|fertilizers]], [[Pesticide|pesticides]], or [[Genetically modified organism|genetically modified organisms]].<ref name=":26">{{Cite journal |last1=Paramasivam |first1=Sivaraj |last2=Henry |first2=Philip |last3=Seethapathy |first3=Parthasarathy |last4=Rajamohan |first4=Thulasiram |date=2 September 2022 |title=A strategic model for empowering farmers by improving livelihood security through organic farming practices in Tamil Nadu, India {{!}} Journal of Agricultural Sciences – Sri Lanka |url=https://jas.sljol.info/articles/10.4038/jas.v17i3.9926 |language=en-US |doi=10.4038/jas.v17i3.9926}}</ref> Organic farming was the norm in India for most of its history, but significant [[Demographics of Africa|population growth]] in the mid-20th century forced farmers to find new ways to provide enough food to support the country.<ref name=":19">{{Cite journal |last1=Dash |first1=Sarthak |last2=Priyadarshini |first2=Sugyanta |last3=Dulla |first3=Nisrutha |date=1 February 2024 |title=Food security and sustainability dimensions of organic farming in the context of India: a comprehensive scientometric review (2010–2023) |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s11356-024-31867-4 |journal=Environmental Science and Pollution Research |language=en |volume=31 |issue=10 |pages=14484–14502 |doi=10.1007/s11356-024-31867-4 |pmid=38305964 |bibcode=2024ESPR...3114484D |issn=1614-7499}}</ref> [[M. S. Swaminathan]], an agricultural scientist, led an initiative known as the [[Green Revolution in India|Green Revolution]] to integrate new technology into existing Indian agrarian practices to increase the farms' yields and general productivity. India began to adopt synthetic fertilizers, pesticides, and new [[Irrigation in India|irrigation]] technology to accomplish this goal. The revolution slowly decreased the frequency of organic farming.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Dasgupta |first=Biplab |date=1977 |title=India's Green Revolution |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/4365324 |journal=Economic and Political Weekly |volume=12 |issue=6/8 |pages=241–260 |jstor=4365324 |issn=0012-9976}}</ref>

==== Current status ====
Due to the Green Revolution, a large majority of farmland in India is not organic. Most Indian farmland is concentrated in large [[Intensive farming|commercial farms]] that prioritise high yields and maximum [[Economy of India|economic gain]].<ref name=":13">{{Cite journal |last1=Dash |first1=Sarthak |last2=Priyadarshini |first2=Sugyanta |last3=Dulla |first3=Nisrutha |date=1 February 2024 |title=Food security and sustainability dimensions of organic farming in the context of India: a comprehensive scientometric review (2010–2023) |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s11356-024-31867-4 |journal=Environmental Science and Pollution Research |language=en |volume=31 |issue=10 |pages=14484–14502 |doi=10.1007/s11356-024-31867-4 |pmid=38305964 |bibcode=2024ESPR...3114484D |issn=1614-7499}}</ref> Organic farmland occupies around 2% of all farmland in India, which is most commonly divided into many small [[Subsistence agriculture|subsistence farms]].<ref name=":13" /> Despite this, India still holds the ninth most organic farmland in the world.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=John Paull |first1=PhD |last2=Hennig |first2=Benjamin D. |date=1 January 2016 |title=Atlas of Organics: Four maps of the world of organic agriculture |url=https://www.academia.edu/25648267 |journal=Journal of Organics}}</ref>

There are several reasons why only a few large-scale organic farms exist in India. Organic farming requires more land, materials, and labour to achieve the same production levels as non-organic farms, so large-scale organic farming is highly inefficient.<ref name=":32">{{Cite journal |last=Singh |first=Ashima |title=OPPORTUNITIES AND CONSTRAINTS IN ORGANIC FARMING: AN INDIAN PERSPECTIVE |url=https://www.academia.edu/31342795}}</ref> Organic agriculture is more expensive and time-consuming compared to conventional farming practices, which further explains the lack of large organic farms.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Norman |first=Siebrecht |date=January 2020 |title=Sustainable Agriculture and Its Implementation Gap—Overcoming Obstacles to Implementation |url=https://www.mdpi.com/2071-1050/12/9/3853 |journal=Sustainability |language=en |volume=12 |issue=9 |doi= |issn=2071-1050 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250430143942/https://www.mdpi.com/2071-1050/12/9/3853 |archive-date=30 April 2025}}</ref>

Organic agriculture has fed [[India]] for centuries and it is again a growing sector in India. ===Infrastructure===
India has very poor rural roads affecting timely supply of inputs and timely transfer of outputs from Indian farms. Irrigation systems are inadequate, leading to crop failures in some parts of the country because of lack of water. In other areas regional floods, poor seed quality and inefficient farming practices, lack of cold storage and harvest spoilage cause over 30% of farmer's produce going to waste, lack of [[Retailing in India|organised retail]] and competing buyers thereby limiting Indian farmer's ability to sell the surplus and commercial crops.

The Indian farmer receives just 10% to 23% of the price the Indian consumer pays for exactly the same produce, the difference going to losses, inefficiencies and middlemen. Farmers in developed economies of Europe and the United States receive 64% to 81%.{{citation needed|date=October 2013}}

===Productivity===
Although India has attained self-sufficiency in food staples, the productivity of its farms is below that of Brazil, the United States, France and other nations. Indian [[wheat]] farms, for example, produce about a third of the wheat per hectare per year compared to farms in France. Rice productivity in India was less than half that of China. Other staples productivity in India is similarly low. Indian [[total factor productivity]] growth remains below 2% per annum; in contrast, China's total factor productivity growths is about 6% per annum, even though China also has [[smallholding]] farmers. Several studies suggest India could eradicate its hunger and malnutrition and be a major source of food for the world by achieving productivity comparable with other countries.{{citation needed|date=October 2013}}

By contrast, Indian farms in some regions post the best yields, for sugarcane, cassava and tea crops.<ref>[http://faostat.fao.org/site/567/DesktopDefault.aspx?PageID=567#ancor Production Crops – Yield by Country] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130114151638/http://faostat.fao.org/site/567/DesktopDefault.aspx?PageID=567 |date=14 January 2013 }}, FAO United Nations 2011</ref>

Crop yields vary significantly between Indian states. Some states produce two to three times more grain per hectare than others.

As the map shows, the traditional regions of high agricultural productivity in India are the north west (Punjab, Haryana and Western Uttar Pradesh), coastal districts on both coasts, West Bengal and Tamil Nadu. Crop yields for some farms in India are within 90% of the best achieved yields by farms in developed countries such as the United States and in European Union. No single state of India is best in every crop. Tamil Nadu achieved highest yields in rice and sugarcane, [[Haryana]] in wheat and coarse grains, Karnataka in cotton, Bihar in pulses, while other states do well in horticulture, aquaculture, flower and fruit plantations. These differences in agricultural productivity are a function of local infrastructure, [[soil quality]], micro-climates, local resources, farmer knowledge and innovations.<ref name=ap1/>

The Indian food distribution system is highly inefficient. Movement of agricultural produce is heavily regulated, with inter-state and even inter-district restrictions on marketing and movement of agricultural goods.<ref name=ap1/>

One study suggests Indian agricultural policy should best focus on improving rural infrastructure primarily in the form of irrigation and flood control infrastructure, knowledge transfer of better yielding and more disease resistant seeds. Additionally, cold storage, hygienic food packaging and efficient modern retail to reduce waste can improve output and rural incomes.<ref name=ap1/>

The low productivity in India is a result of the following factors:
* The average size of land holdings is very small (less than 2 hectares) and is subject to fragmentation due to land ceiling acts, and in some cases, family disputes. Such small holdings are often over-manned, resulting in disguised unemployment and low productivity of labour. Some reports claim smallholder farming may not be cause of poor productivity, since the productivity is higher in China and many developing economies even though China smallholder farmers constitute over 97% of its farming population.<ref>{{Cite FTP |title=Rapid growth of select Asian economies|year=2006|server=Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations|url-status=dead|url=ftp://ftp.fao.org/docrep/fao/009/ag087e/ag087e00.pdf}}</ref> A Chinese smallholder farmer is able to rent his land to larger farmers, China's organised retail and extensive Chinese highways are able to provide the incentive and infrastructure necessary to its farmers for sharp increases in farm productivity.
* Adoption of modern agricultural practices and use of [[Agricultural machinery|technology]] is inadequate in comparison with Green Revolution methods and technologies, hampered by ignorance of such practices, high costs and impracticality in the case of small land holdings.
* According to the [[World Bank]], Indian branch's ''Priorities for Agriculture and Rural Development'', India's large [[agricultural subsidies]] are hampering productivity-enhancing investment. This evaluation is based largely on a productivity agenda and does not take any ecological implications into account. According to a neo-liberal view, over-regulation of agriculture has increased costs, price risks and uncertainty because the government intervenes in labour, land, and credit markets. India has inadequate infrastructure and services.<ref name="agriculturepriorities">{{cite web|url=http://web.worldbank.org/WBSITE/EXTERNAL/COUNTRIES/SOUTHASIAEXT/EXTSAREGTOPAGRI/0,,contentMDK:20273764~menuPK:548214~pagePK:34004173~piPK:34003707~theSitePK:452766,00.html|title=India: Priorities for Agriculture and Rural Development|publisher=World Bank|access-date=8 January 2009|archive-date=21 January 2009|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090121122011/http://web.worldbank.org/WBSITE/EXTERNAL/COUNTRIES/SOUTHASIAEXT/EXTSAREGTOPAGRI/0,,contentMDK:20273764~menuPK:548214~pagePK:34004173~piPK:34003707~theSitePK:452766,00.html|url-status=live}}</ref> The World Bank also says that the allocation of water is inefficient, unsustainable and inequitable. The policy suggested that, as far as possible, land with low farming yields or that was not farmable should be earmarked for non-agricultural purposes such as construction, industrial parks and other commercial development.<ref name="policy2007"/>

[[Amartya Sen]] offered a counter viewpoint, stating that "prohibiting the use of agricultural land for commercial and industrial development is ultimately self-defeating".<ref name="telegraphindia.com">The Telegraph. 23 July 2007 [https://web.archive.org/web/20070930041624/http://www.telegraphindia.com/1070723/asp/nation/story_8094453.asp 'Prohibiting the use of agricultural land for industries is ultimately self-defeating']</ref> He stated that agricultural land may be better suited for non-agriculture purposes if industrial production could generate many times more than the value of the product produced by agriculture.<ref name="telegraphindia.com"/> Sen suggested India needed to bring productive industry everywhere, wherever there are advantages of production, market needs and the locational preferences of managers, engineers, technical experts as well as unskilled labour because of education, healthcare and other infrastructure. He stated that instead of government controlling land allocation based on soil characteristics, the market economy should determine productive allocation of land.<ref name="telegraphindia.com"/>

Startups with niche technology and new business models are working to solve problems in Indian agriculture and its marketing.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.techinasia.com/real-indian-startups-will-be-in-agriculture|title=Tech in Asia – Connecting Asia's startup ecosystem|website=www.techinasia.com|language=en-US|access-date=4 June 2016|archive-date=30 June 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160630204158/https://www.techinasia.com/real-indian-startups-will-be-in-agriculture|url-status=live}}</ref> Kandawale is one such e-commerce website which sells Indian red onions to bulk users direct from farmers, reducing unnecessary cost escalations.

In July 2025, the [[Government of India]] launched the [[Prime minister|Prime Minister]] Dhan-Dhaanya Krishi Yojana, a six-year initiative with an annual outlay of ₹24,000 crore, aimed at boosting crop yields and [[Farmer|farmers]]' income in 100 low-performing districts.

Starting from the 2025–26 rabi season, the scheme will benefit around 1.7 crore [[Farmer|farmers]] through convergence of 36 existing schemes across multiple ministries. It focuses on [[crop diversification]], sustainable practices, [[irrigation]], storage infrastructure, and improved access to credit.

District-level plans, monitored through 117 key indicators, will align with national goals of self-reliance, [[organic farming]], and increased [[Agriculture|agricultural]] productivity. The initiative is a major step towards achieving [[Atmanirbhar Bharat]] in the [[agriculture sector]].<ref>{{cite magazine |title=Govt clears farm scheme with Rs 24k cr annual outlay for 6 yrs to be implemented from Oct |url=https://www.theweek.in/wire-updates/national/2025/07/16/del66-cab-2ndld-agri.html |magazine=The Week |agency=PTI |date=16 July 2025 |access-date=17 July 2025}}</ref>

=== Agriculture and the Indian economy ===

The contributions of agriculture in the Indian economy have been increasing over the years. According to the economic survey, the share of agriculture in gross domestic product (GDP) reached almost 20% for the first time in 17 years, making a sole bright spot in performance during financial year 2020–2021.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Agri share in GDP hit 20% after 17 years: Economic Survey|url=https://www.downtoearth.org.in/news/agriculture/agri-share-in-gdp-hit-20-after-17-years-economic-survey-75271|access-date=28 March 2021|website=www.downtoearth.org.in|date=29 January 2021|language=en|archive-date=18 April 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210418182103/https://www.downtoearth.org.in/news/agriculture/agri-share-in-gdp-hit-20-after-17-years-economic-survey-75271|url-status=live}}</ref>

Modern farms and agriculture operations have changed over the years primarily because of advancements in technology, including sensors, devices, machines, and information technology.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Agriculture Technology {{!}} National Institute of Food and Agriculture|url=https://www.nifa.usda.gov/topics/agriculture-technology|access-date=28 March 2021|website=nifa.usda.gov|archive-date=5 March 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210305145704/https://nifa.usda.gov/topic/agriculture-technology|url-status=live}}</ref>

Personalized e-commerce stores and market places have brought farming products like fertilizers, seeds, machines and equipment that help farmers grow quality products. Educational portals let farmers know innovative things about farming that increase the contributions of agriculture to the economy.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Applying modern tech to agriculture|url=https://www.downtoearth.org.in/blog/agriculture/applying-modern-tech-to-agriculture-66017|access-date=28 March 2021|website=www.downtoearth.org.in|date=5 August 2019|language=en|archive-date=29 January 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210129063905/https://www.downtoearth.org.in/blog/agriculture/applying-modern-tech-to-agriculture-66017|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=E-Commerce for Ag Business: Advantages and Challenges|url=https://extension.psu.edu/e-commerce-for-ag-business-advantages-and-challenges|access-date=28 March 2021|website=Penn State Extension|language=en|archive-date=14 March 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210314083401/https://extension.psu.edu/e-commerce-for-ag-business-advantages-and-challenges|url-status=live}}</ref>

[[Indian companies]] such as [[JCBL Agri(agricultural machinery parts exporter)|JCBL Agri]], part of the [[JCBL Group]], manufacture and export [[agricultural machinery]] replacement parts, supplying components for various [[farm equipment]] used in domestic and [[international markets]].

=== Organic farming ===

==== Historical initiatives ====
The [[Green Revolution in India|Green Revolution's]] shift to new farming methods, such as irrigation and synthetic fertilizers, led to negative effects on the [[Environment of India|environment]].<ref name=":22">{{Cite journal |last1=Paramasivam |first1=Sivaraj |last2=Henry |first2=Philip |last3=Seethapathy |first3=Parthasarathy |last4=Rajamohan |first4=Thulasiram |date=2 September 2022 |title=A strategic model for empowering farmers by improving livelihood security through organic farming practices in Tamil Nadu, India {{!}} Journal of Agricultural Sciences – Sri Lanka |url=https://jas.sljol.info/articles/10.4038/jas.v17i3.9926 |language=en-US |doi=10.4038/jas.v17i3.9926}}</ref> The rise of commercial farms to support the Indian population, coupled with demands from other countries, resulted in mass [[Deforestation in India|deforestation]]. Excess water from irrigation systems collects [[Pesticide poisoning|toxic chemicals]] from pesticides, leading to [[Runoff model (reservoir)|runoff]] into streams that kills [[Wildlife of India|wildlife]] and pollutes [[Water resources|freshwater sources]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Niggli |first=Urs |date=February 2015 |title=Sustainability of organic food production: challenges and innovations |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/proceedings-of-the-nutrition-society/article/sustainability-of-organic-food-production-challenges-and-innovations/AC943956EBE48385706EAB58DEF71BB5 |journal=Proceedings of the Nutrition Society |language=en |volume=74 |issue=1 |pages=83–88 |doi=10.1017/S0029665114001438 |pmid=25221987 |issn=0029-6651}}</ref> These and other effects have prompted concerns about the [[sustainability]] of non-organic farming, thereby raising awareness about the importance of adopting more [[Sustainable agriculture|sustainable organic farming practices]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Gabriel |first1=Doreen |last2=Sait |first2=Steven M. |last3=Kunin |first3=William E. |last4=Benton |first4=Tim G. |date=2013 |title=Food production vs. biodiversity: comparing organic and conventional agriculture |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/1365-2664.12035 |journal=Journal of Applied Ecology |language=en |volume=50 |issue=2 |pages=355–364 |doi=10.1111/1365-2664.12035 |bibcode=2013JApEc..50..355G |issn=1365-2664}}</ref>

One leader of this development was [[Albert Howard|Sir Albert Howard.]] He was an English [[Botany|botanist]] who helped advance organic agricultural developments through numerous publications on sustainable organic farming methods in India.<ref name=":34">{{Cite journal |last=Singh |first=Ashima |title=OPPORTUNITIES AND CONSTRAINTS IN ORGANIC FARMING: AN INDIAN PERSPECTIVE |url=https://www.academia.edu/31342795}}</ref> He raised awareness about the adverse effects of non-organic farming on the environment and helped educate the Indian population about the benefits of organic farming. His work and contributions to the field of organic agriculture led him to be known as the founder of the organic farming movement.<ref name=":34" />

==== Recent initiatives ====
With the recent concerns about [[Herbicide|non-organic farming practices]] and their possibly adverse health effects, there has been a noticeable increase in demand for [[organic food]] in India.<ref name=":14">{{Cite journal |last1=Dash |first1=Sarthak |last2=Priyadarshini |first2=Sugyanta |last3=Dulla |first3=Nisrutha |date=1 February 2024 |title=Food security and sustainability dimensions of organic farming in the context of India: a comprehensive scientometric review (2010–2023) |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s11356-024-31867-4 |journal=Environmental Science and Pollution Research |language=en |volume=31 |issue=10 |pages=14484–14502 |doi=10.1007/s11356-024-31867-4 |pmid=38305964 |bibcode=2024ESPR...3114484D |issn=1614-7499}}</ref> As more people notice the negative effects of non-organic farming on sustainability, it contributes to grow the organic farming movement. [[Government of India|The Government of India]] is also playing an active role in promoting organic agriculture, as its various initiatives, like Paramparagat Krishi Vikas Yojana and zero-budget natural farming, are making organic farming more accessible and sustainable.<ref name=":14" /> Most initiatives now focus on how organic agriculture can lead to improvements in the country's sustainability.

Paramparagat Krishi Vikas Yojana (PKVY) was launched in 2015 by the [[Narendra Modi]] regime to promote organic farming, under which farmers form organic farming clusters of 50 or more farmers with a minimum total area of {{convert|50|acre|order=flip}} to share organic methods using traditional sustainable methods, costs, and [[marketing]], etc.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Paramparagat Krishi Vikas Yojana {{!}} District South West, Government of Delhi {{!}} India |url=https://dmsouthwest.delhi.gov.in/scheme/paramparagat-krishi-vikas-yojana/ |access-date=12 October 2025 |language=en-US}}</ref> It initially aimed to have 10,000 clusters by 2018 with at least {{convert|500,000|acre|order=flip}} under organic farming. It also aimed for the government to cover certification costs while promoting the use of traditional resources in organic farming. The government provides {{convert|20,000|$/acre|$/ha|$=₹|abbr=off|order=flip}} or {{convert|{{To USD|20000|IND|year=2019}}|$/acre|$/ha|$=US$|abbr=off|order=flip}} benefit over three years.<ref name=ins1>[https://www.indiatoday.in/education-today/gk-current-affairs/story/10-important-government-schemes-agriculture-sector-divd-1593413-2019-08-30 10 important government schemes for agriculture sector] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210723104804/https://www.indiatoday.in/education-today/gk-current-affairs/story/10-important-government-schemes-agriculture-sector-divd-1593413-2019-08-30 |date=23 July 2021 }}, India today, 30 August 2019.</ref>

Other techniques of organic farming like [[Zero Budget Natural Farming|zero budget natural farming]] (ZBNF) have been implemented by many small-scale farmers in [[Wayanad district|Wayanad]], Kerala.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Khadse |first1=Ashlesha |last2=Rosset |first2=Peter M. |date=September 2019 |title=Zero Budget Natural Farming in India – from inception to institutionalization |url=https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2019AgSFS..43..848K/abstract |journal=Agroecology and Sustainable Food Systems |language=en |volume=43 |issue=7–8 |pages=848–871 |doi=10.1080/21683565.2019.1608349 |bibcode=2019AgSFS..43..848K |issn=2168-3565}}</ref> In this process they implement more natural and ecological methods of farming that decrease or completely cease use of pesticides and damaging chemicals. This alleviates damage caused by chemical overuse and mono cropping which is depleting the formerly fertile forest-land in the area.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Münster |first=Daniel |date=March 2017 |title=Zero Budget Natural Farming and Bovine Entanglements in South India |url=http://www.environmentandsociety.org/node/7771/ |journal=RCC Perspectives: Transformations in Environment and Society |issue=1 |pages=25–32 |language=en |doi=10.5282/RCC/7771 |access-date=29 April 2023 |archive-date=13 September 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240913065712/https://www.environmentandsociety.org/perspectives/2017/1/article/zero-budget-natural-farming-and-bovine-entanglements-south-india |url-status=live }}</ref>

One specific initiative is increasing the availability of [[organic farming]] in [[Tamil Nadu]].<ref name=":24">{{Cite book |last=Commissionerate of Municipal Administration |first=Government of Tamil Nadu |title=Disposal of the Wet Waste Through Micro Composting Centres (MCC) |publisher=Commissionerate of Municipal Administration, Government of Tamil Nadu |location=Chennai, Tamil Nadu, India |pages=1-18 |language=en}}</ref> [[Government of Tamil Nadu|The Government of Tamil Nadu]] has been publishing resources for farmers in the state to reduce their dependence on chemical fertilizers like Diammonium Phosphate and Urea.<ref name=":24" /> One specific resource outlines the creation of [[Compost|micro-compositing centers]], also known as decentralized compositing centers. These are centers all around Tamil Nadu that turn people’s trash into compost and cleaning supplies.<ref name=":24" />

An example of an existing center is [[Chennai]] Composting Center.<ref name=":33">{{Cite web |title=Compost Connect – Namma Ooru Foundation |url=https://nammaooru.org/compost-connect/ |access-date=2025-12-13 |language=en-GB}}</ref> This is a Micro Composting Center that repurposes one ton of trash and turns it into organic compost every day for large suppliers and [[Farm|farms]] around Chennai.<ref name=":33" /> By repurposing trash into compost to reduce [[fertilizer]] use in the area, Chennai Composting Center is creating a more [[Sustainable agriculture|sustainable]] agricultural community.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Radhakrishnan |first=Shobana |date=2025-04-25 |title=What stench? Chennai composting centre turns trash into treasure, minus the smell |url=https://citizenmatters.in/micro-composting-centre-chennai-waste-300-tonnes-compost-windrow-composting-namma-ooru-gcc/ |access-date=2025-12-13 |website=Citizen Matters |language=en-US}}</ref>

Along with progression with organic farming methods, new technologies in the form of [[Hygrometer|moisture sensors]] and [[Artificial intelligence in agriculture|artificial intelligence]] are also being implemented in the Indian farming sector. Farmers are using moisture sensors to ensure that different crops have the exact amount of water that they need, which ensures that farmers can maximise crop yield.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Marcus |first=Hardie |date=2020–2021 |title=Review of Novel and Emerging Proximal Soil Moisture Sensors for Use in Agriculture |journal=Sensors |language=en |volume=20 |issue=23 |page=6934 |doi=10.3390/s20236934 |pmid=33291606 |pmc=7730258 |bibcode=2020Senso..20.6934H |doi-access=free |issn=1424-8220 }}</ref> Along with this, artificial intelligence techniques are being implemented in [[Food processing|food processing plants]] across India. AI provides more efficient ways to produce, harvest, and sell crops products as well as an emphasis on checking defective crops and improving the potential for healthy crop production.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Jha |first1=Kirtan |last2=Doshi |first2=Aalap |last3=Patel |first3=Poojan |last4=Shah |first4=Manan |date=1 June 2019 |title=A comprehensive review on automation in agriculture using artificial intelligence |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2589721719300182 |journal=Artificial Intelligence in Agriculture |volume=2 |pages=1–12 |doi=10.1016/j.aiia.2019.05.004 |issn=2589-7217}}</ref> This further helps maximise crop yield as Rayda Ayed describes in her research on the effects of artificial intelligence in India.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ben Ayed |first1=Rayda |last2=Hanana |first2=Mohsen |date=22 April 2021 |title=Artificial Intelligence to Improve the Food and Agriculture Sector |journal=Journal of Food Quality |language=en |volume=2021 |article-number=e5584754 |doi=10.1155/2021/5584754 |issn=0146-9428 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

==== Sustainability ====
Organic farming practices are currently having a positive effect on India's environment and will further improve the country's sustainability if continued. Specifically, it has a direct link to improving the [[Economy of India|economic]] sustainability of non-commercial farmers.<ref name=":15">{{Cite journal |last1=Dash |first1=Sarthak |last2=Priyadarshini |first2=Sugyanta |last3=Dulla |first3=Nisrutha |date=1 February 2024 |title=Food security and sustainability dimensions of organic farming in the context of India: a comprehensive scientometric review (2010–2023) |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s11356-024-31867-4 |journal=Environmental Science and Pollution Research |language=en |volume=31 |issue=10 |pages=14484–14502 |doi=10.1007/s11356-024-31867-4 |pmid=38305964 |bibcode=2024ESPR...3114484D |issn=1614-7499}}</ref> Organic farmers can sell products on a small scale at a higher price than non-organic products. This enables them to increase their earnings on food sales and achieve greater economic sustainability.<ref name=":15" /> Further, organic farming is also creating more jobs in rural areas, as organic farms require more labour compared to non-organic ones.<ref name=":23">{{Cite journal |last1=Paramasivam |first1=Sivaraj |last2=Henry |first2=Philip |last3=Seethapathy |first3=Parthasarathy |last4=Rajamohan |first4=Thulasiram |date=2 September 2022 |title=A strategic model for empowering farmers by improving livelihood security through organic farming practices in Tamil Nadu, India {{!}} Journal of Agricultural Sciences – Sri Lanka |url=https://jas.sljol.info/articles/10.4038/jas.v17i3.9926 |language=en-US |doi=10.4038/jas.v17i3.9926}}</ref>

This applies to two specific fertilizers used in India, [[Urea]] and [[Diammonium phosphate|Diammonium Phosphate]] (DAP).<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Randive |first=Kirtikumar |last2=Raut |first2=Tejashree |last3=Jawadand |first3=Sanjeevani |date=2021-10-01 |title=An overview of the global fertilizer trends and India’s position in 2020 |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s13563-020-00246-z |journal=Mineral Economics |language=en |volume=34 |issue=3 |pages=371–384 |doi=10.1007/s13563-020-00246-z |issn=2191-2211}}</ref> Urea is the most imported fertilizer in India, and it has many adverse health effects on those who use it.<ref name=":04">{{Cite journal |last=Dickerson |first=Aisha S. |last2=Lee |first2=Janice S. |last3=Keshava |first3=Channa |last4=Hotchkiss |first4=Andrew |last5=Persad |first5=Amanda S. |date=2018-06-01 |title=Assessment of Health Effects of Exogenous Urea: Summary and Key Findings |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s40572-018-0198-8 |journal=Current Environmental Health Reports |language=en |volume=5 |issue=2 |pages=205–212 |doi=10.1007/s40572-018-0198-8 |issn=2196-5412 |pmc=9161740 |pmid=29713991}}</ref> When these fertilizers come into contact with uncovered skin, they can cause [[irritation]] and, if left untreated, lead to skin damage.<ref name=":17">{{Cite journal |last=Prasad |first=Rajendra |date=1998 |title=Fertilizer urea, food security, health and the environment |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/24101710 |journal=Current Science |volume=75 |issue=7 |pages=677–683 |issn=0011-3891}}</ref> Diammonium Phosphate also causes similar effects when it comes into contact with uncovered skin and eyes.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Diammonium Phosphate (DAP) Safety Data Sheet |url=https://www.cropnutrition.com/resource-library/diammonium-phosphate-dap-safety-data-sheet/ |access-date=2025-12-13 |website=Mosaic Crop Nutrition |language=en-US}}</ref> Skin irritation comes from these fertilizers releasing compounds such as [[Ammonia pollution|ammonia]] and [[Agricultural pollution|nitrogen oxides]], which are harmful to both the human body and the [[Soil erosion|soil]] they are applied to.<ref name=":04" />

Regarding the environment, Urea, Diammonium Phosphate, and other fertilizers in India increase atmospheric nitrogen levels and [[Soil erosion|strip soil of its nutrients]].<ref name=":17" /> When these fertilizers are spread along farms, they react with water and release ammonia, which increases the amount of nitrogen in the air, and carbon dioxide into the atmosphere.<ref name=":17" /> This causes air and soil pollution, with adverse long-term effects.<ref name=":04" /> The continued use of these fertilizers is damaging [[Environment of India|India's environment]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Randive |first=Kirtikumar |last2=Raut |first2=Tejashree |last3=Jawadand |first3=Sanjeevani |date=2021-10-01 |title=An overview of the global fertilizer trends and India’s position in 2020 |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s13563-020-00246-z |journal=Mineral Economics |language=en |volume=34 |issue=3 |pages=371–384 |doi=10.1007/s13563-020-00246-z |issn=2191-2211}}</ref>

In terms of [[Environmental Performance Index|environmental sustainability]], organic farms do not use any artificial pesticides or fertilizers. This means that there is no toxic runoff or other environmentally damaging effects from organic farms.<ref name=":23" /> Avoiding these dangerous chemicals also leads to a healthier environment for farmers, as they do not have to deal with any threatening chemicals.<ref name=":15" />

==== The future of organic agriculture ====
Organic farming has a combination of positive and negative outlooks in India. On the positive side, organic farming's high levels of sustainability offer it a promising future. Organic farms contribute to safer and healthier lives for both farmers and consumers due to their lack of dangerous chemicals, making the industry's projected outlook long-lasting and promising.<ref name=":16">{{Cite journal |last1=Dash |first1=Sarthak |last2=Priyadarshini |first2=Sugyanta |last3=Dulla |first3=Nisrutha |date=1 February 2024 |title=Food security and sustainability dimensions of organic farming in the context of India: a comprehensive scientometric review (2010–2023) |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s11356-024-31867-4 |journal=Environmental Science and Pollution Research |language=en |volume=31 |issue=10 |pages=14484–14502 |doi=10.1007/s11356-024-31867-4 |pmid=38305964 |bibcode=2024ESPR...3114484D |issn=1614-7499}}</ref>

On the other hand, organic farms have some adverse effects. For example, organic farms have lower yields compared to non-organic farms. Compensating for this issue results in organic farmers cultivating more land to produce similar amounts of crops.<ref name=":03">{{Cite journal |last=Niggli |first=Urs |date=February 2015 |title=Sustainability of organic food production: challenges and innovations |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/proceedings-of-the-nutrition-society/article/sustainability-of-organic-food-production-challenges-and-innovations/AC943956EBE48385706EAB58DEF71BB5 |journal=Proceedings of the Nutrition Society |language=en |volume=74 |issue=1 |pages=83–88 |doi=10.1017/S0029665114001438 |pmid=25221987 |issn=0029-6651}}</ref> This leads to deforestation, which is not sustainable. The ideal form of agriculture in India calls for a combination of both organic and [[Agriculture|non-organic farming techniques]] to maximise yields while promoting economic and environmental sustainability.<ref name=":03" />

[[Category:Agriculture in India| ]]
extract:
The history of agriculture in India dates back to the Neolithic period. India ranks second worldwide in farm outputs. As per the Indian economic survey 2020–21, agriculture employed more than 50% of the Indian workforce and contributed 20.2% to the country's GDP.
In 2016, agriculture and allied sectors like animal husbandry, forestry and fisheries accounted for 17.5% of the GDP (gross domestic product) with about 41.49% of the workforce in 2020. India ranks first in the world with highest net cropped area followed by US and China. The economic contribution of agriculture to India's GDP is steadily declining with the country's broad-based economic growth. Still, agriculture is demographically the broadest economic sector and plays a significant role in the overall socio-economic fabric of India.
The total agriculture commodities export was US$3.50 billion in March–June 2020. India exported $38 billion worth of agricultural products in 2013, making it the seventh-largest agricultural exporter worldwide and the sixth largest net exporter. Most of its agriculture exports serve developing and least developed nations. Indian agricultural/horticultural and processed foods are exported to more than 120 countries, primarily to Japan, Southeast Asia, SAARC countries, the European Union and the United States.
Pesticides and fertilizers used in Indian agriculture have helped increase crop productivity, but their unregulated and excessive use has caused different ecosystem and fatal health problems. Several studies published between 2011 and 2020 attribute 45 different types of cancers afflicting rural farm workers in India to pesticide usage. The chemicals have been shown to cause DNA damage, hormone disruption, and lead to a weakened immune system. Occupational exposure to pesticides has been identified as a major trigger of the development of cancer. The principal classes of pesticides investigated in relation to their role in intoxication and cancer were insecticides, herbicides, and fungicides. Punjab, a state in India, utilises the highest amount of chemical fertilizers in the country. Many of the pesticides sprayed on the state's crops are classified as class I by the World Health Organization because of their acute toxicity and are banned in places around the world, including Europe.
